Momentum is one of the most important and fundamental quantities in physics. It is conserved in all interactions — from subatomic particle collisions to car crashes to the explosion of stars. In this lesson, we will define momentum, explore the law of conservation of momentum, study different types of collisions, and introduce the concept of impulse. We will also see how the physics of momentum informs important safety features in vehicles.

This law applies to all interactions: collisions, explosions, and any event where objects exert forces on each other. It is one of the most fundamental laws in physics and holds true even when energy is not conserved (as in inelastic collisions).

By Newton's third law, when two objects interact, they exert equal and opposite forces on each other. They interact for the same duration of time. Therefore, the change in momentum of one object is equal and opposite to the change in momentum of the other. The total momentum of the system does not change.
, both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. The objects bounce off each other, and no energy is converted to heat, sound, or deformation.

Perfectly elastic collisions are rare in everyday life. They occur approximately in collisions between hard objects (like steel balls or billiard balls) and precisely in collisions between atoms or molecules.

Most real-world collisions are inelastic. Car crashes, a ball hitting the ground, and a football being kicked are all inelastic collisions.

This principle is the basis of many safety features:
The front and rear of a car are designed to crumple (deform) in a collision. This extends the time over which the car decelerates, reducing the force on the occupants.

Seatbelts are slightly elastic and stretch during a collision. This increases the time over which the person decelerates, reducing the force on the body. Without a seatbelt, the person would hit the dashboard or windscreen and stop almost instantaneously — a very short time means a very large force.
Airbags inflate during a collision and slowly deflate as the person's head and chest push into them. This extends the stopping time, reducing the force.
Helmets contain a layer of crushable foam. In an impact, the foam compresses, increasing the time over which the head decelerates and reducing the force on the skull.
Soft, padded surfaces increase the stopping time when a child falls, reducing the impact force.
Bending the knees when landing from a jump:
By bending your knees, you increase the time over which you decelerate, reducing the force on your legs and joints.

"Momentum and kinetic energy are the same."
) are different quantities. Momentum is a vector and is always conserved in collisions. Kinetic energy is a scalar and is only conserved in elastic collisions.
"Momentum is not conserved in inelastic collisions."
Momentum is ALWAYS conserved in all types of collisions (provided there are no external forces). What is not conserved in inelastic collisions is kinetic energy.
"A heavier object always has more momentum."
Momentum depends on both mass and velocity. A light object moving very fast can have more momentum than a heavy object moving slowly.
Momentum is not created or destroyed. In an explosion starting from rest, the total momentum remains zero — the momenta of the fragments are equal and opposite and sum to zero.
"Objects always bounce off each other in collisions."
In perfectly inelastic collisions, objects stick together. Not all collisions involve bouncing.
"Crumple zones reduce the change in momentum."
